The model generates output one token at a time. Greedily taking the single most probable token at each step is the simplest option, and it can lock in an early mistake that a slightly less probable first choice would have avoided.

Beam search keeps several options alive instead. It carries a 'beam' of the $k$ highest-scoring partial sequences, and here $k=4$.

Each step follows the same cycle. Every sequence in the beam is extended by each plausible next token. The resulting candidates are scored by their accumulated log-probability. Only the top $k$ survive into the next step.

A sequence that produces the end-of-sequence token stops growing and becomes a finished candidate. The best finished candidate is the output.

Two further decoding settings go with it: a [[length-penalty]] of $\alpha = 0.6$, and a cap on output length at input length + 50, with early termination when possible.

Beam size and length penalty were chosen on the development set. Beam size was also one of the few hyperparameters re-tuned for [[constituency-parsing]].

concepts.name: Length penalty (alpha = 0.6)
concepts.summary: A normalization applied to beam-search scores so that longer output sequences are not unfairly penalized; the paper uses strength alpha = 0.6 from the GNMT paper.
concepts.explanation:
[[beam-search]] scores a candidate sequence by summing the log-probability of each token it emitted. Every one of those log-probabilities is negative, so each additional token drives the running total further down. A longer candidate therefore ends up with a worse score than a shorter one partly just because it is longer, and plain beam search drifts toward short outputs.

The length penalty corrects for that. Each candidate's score is divided by a term that grows with the candidate's length, so the accumulated negative sum is normalized against the number of tokens that produced it. An exponent $\alpha$ sets how strong the correction is; at $\alpha = 0$ the divisor is constant and there is no correction at all.

The paper does not restate the formula. It takes both the formulation and the value $\alpha = 0.6$ from [38].

citedFrom.refText: Wu et al. Google's neural machine translation system. arXiv:1609.08144, 2016.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The exact length-penalty formula, and the early-termination inference procedure the paper says it follows, are defined in [38].

concepts.name: Maximum output length rule
concepts.summary: During inference the output is capped at input length + 50 tokens, with early termination when possible.
concepts.explanation:
Decoding needs a stopping rule that does not depend on the model behaving well. The paper sets a hard ceiling: generation never runs past the input length plus 50 tokens.

That ceiling is only an upper bound. When the beam finishes naturally the decoder stops earlier, following the procedure of [38].

The rule does two things at once. It keeps a model that fails to emit an end-of-sequence token from generating indefinitely, and it puts a fixed bound on the compute any single inference call can consume.

concepts.name: Checkpoint averaging
concepts.summary: The final model's weights are the elementwise average of the last several saved checkpoints: 5 for base models, 20 for big models, written at 10-minute intervals.
concepts.explanation:
A checkpoint is a snapshot of all model weights, written to disk partway through training. In these runs a checkpoint was written every 10 minutes.

The obvious thing to evaluate is the very last checkpoint — the weights exactly as they stood when training stopped. The paper does something else. It takes the last several checkpoints and averages their parameters elementwise: the last 5 for base models, the last 20 for big models.

Late in training the weights are still moving from step to step, and much of that motion is noise rather than progress. Averaging several nearby checkpoints smooths that step-to-step noise out. It also acts like a cheap ensemble, with the difference that the average is a single set of weights, so inference still costs what one model costs.

All reported translation results use these averaged models.

concepts.name: Training-cost FLOPs estimate
concepts.summary: The paper estimates each model's training cost as training time x number of GPUs x an assumed sustained single-precision throughput per GPU.
concepts.explanation:
The papers being compared here trained on different hardware, so wall-clock hours do not mean the same thing from one row to the next. To put them on a common footing, the paper converts every training run into estimated floating point operations.

The conversion is a product of three terms. Take the wall-clock training time, multiply by the number of GPUs, and multiply by an assumed sustained single-precision throughput for that GPU model. The assumed throughputs are 2.8, 3.7, 6.0, and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40, and P100 GPUs respectively.

Those throughput figures are assumptions rather than measurements taken during the runs. The resulting numbers are therefore estimates, not measured costs.

On this basis the paper claims its models cost a fraction of competing models to train — the big English-French model, for example, at less than 1/4 the previous state of the art's cost.

concepts.name: Model variation ablations (Table 3)
concepts.summary: Experiments that change one component of the base model at a time and measure the effect on English-to-German translation, to see which parts matter.
concepts.explanation:
Section 6.2 asks which parts of the base Transformer actually matter. The method is one knob at a time: vary a single component, hold the rest of the model fixed, and report perplexity and BLEU for each resulting variant on English-to-German.

Table 3 groups the variants by which knob was turned. Rows (A) vary the number of attention heads, and find a sweet spot rather than a straight-line trend. Rows (B) shrink the attention key size $d_k$, which hurts quality.

Rows (C) and (D) cover scale and regularization: bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful against over-fitting. Row (E) swaps the [[sinusoidal-positional-encoding]] for [[learned-positional-embedding|learned positional embeddings]] and changes almost nothing.

Each of these findings is a child concept.

concepts.name: Number of heads sweet spot
concepts.summary: Varying the head count with total computation held constant shows single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, but too many heads also degrades quality.
concepts.explanation:
Rows (A) of Table 3 vary the number of attention heads $h$. The comparison is arranged so that head count is the only thing that really changes: as $h$ grows, the per-head key and value dimensions $d_k, d_v$ shrink in proportion, which holds total computation constant. That is the setup described in section 3.2.2.

At the low end, a single head scores 0.9 BLEU below the best configuration. Splitting attention across several heads earns its place.

The trend does not simply continue upward, though. Quality also drops with too many heads, the regime in which each individual head is working in a very low-dimensional space. The base model's $h = 8$ sits in the effective middle.

concepts.name: Reducing d_k hurts quality
concepts.summary: Shrinking the attention key dimension d_k lowers translation quality, suggesting the dot product may be too simple a compatibility function.
concepts.explanation:
Rows (B) of Table 3 reduce $d_k$. That is the dimension of the query and key vectors — the pair whose dot product decides how much attention one position pays to another — so $d_k$ is the width of the space in which compatibility gets judged.

Shrinking that space lowers model quality.

The paper reads this as evidence that 'determining compatibility is not easy'. A dot product taken in fewer dimensions has less capacity to express which positions should attend to which. From there the paper suggests that a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial.

That last step is a hedge, not a demonstrated result. The ablation shows the drop; it does not show that a different compatibility function would recover it.

concepts.name: Model size and dropout effects
concepts.summary: Bigger models translate better, and dropout is very helpful in preventing over-fitting.
concepts.explanation:
Rows (C) and (D) of Table 3 vary two things whose behaviour the paper calls expected, and both confirm the expectation.

Rows (C) change model size — dimensions such as $d_{model}$ and the feed-forward width. Increasing them improves quality.

Rows (D) change dropout. Removing or reducing it hurts quality, which the paper attributes to over-fitting.

Together these rows are what justifies the big model configuration and the $P_{drop}$ choices in the training recipe.

concepts.name: English constituency parsing
concepts.summary: The task of producing a sentence's syntactic tree — nested phrases like noun phrases and verb phrases — used as a generalization test for the Transformer beyond translation.
concepts.explanation:
Constituency parsing takes a sentence and produces a tree over it. The tree groups words into labeled phrases and nests those phrases inside one another — a noun phrase inside a verb phrase inside a sentence.

To put this through a sequence-to-sequence model, the tree is written out as a bracketed sequence. That output is significantly longer than the input, and it is not free-form: brackets have to nest and close correctly or the sequence does not denote a tree at all. Strong structural constraints on the output are precisely what translation does not impose.

The paper picks the task for that reason, and for a second one. RNN sequence-to-sequence models had not reached state-of-the-art results on parsing in small-data regimes.

The model is a 4-layer Transformer with $d_{model}=1024$. Only three things were re-tuned for the task — dropout, learning rate, and beam size — using the WSJ Section 22 development set.

It outperforms all previously reported models except the [[recurrent-neural-network-grammar]]. Trained only on the 40K-sentence WSJ set, it still beats the BerkeleyParser — a regime where RNN seq2seq models had struggled.

concepts.name: Penn Treebank (WSJ portion)
concepts.summary: The standard constituency-parsing dataset: about 40K hand-parsed sentences from the Wall Street Journal.
concepts.explanation:
The Penn Treebank is a corpus of English sentences annotated with syntactic trees by linguists.

Its Wall Street Journal portion is the standard supervised training set for [[constituency-parsing|English constituency parsing]]: about 40K training sentences. Section 22 of that portion is the development set, and it is the set the paper tuned on.

40K sentences is small by neural standards. That is exactly what makes the WSJ-only result a small-data test rather than a demonstration at scale.

For this setting the paper uses a 16K-token vocabulary.

citedFrom.refText: Marcus, Marcinkiewicz & Santorini. Building a large annotated corpus of English: the Penn Treebank. 1993.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The dataset's construction and standard splits (training sections, Section 22 dev, Section 23 test) are defined in [25].

concepts.name: Semi-supervised parsing setting
concepts.summary: A second training regime that adds about 17M automatically parsed sentences from the high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora on top of the WSJ data.
concepts.explanation:
The WSJ portion supplies about 40K sentences whose trees were annotated by hand. The paper also trains in a second regime, with far more data.

That regime adds roughly 17 million further sentences. Their parse trees were produced by existing parsers rather than by humans — the 'high-confidence' and BerkeleyParser corpora used in prior sequence-to-sequence parsing work.

That is the sense in which the setting is semi-supervised. The extra sentences do carry labels, but machine-generated ones.

The vocabulary grows to 32K tokens for this setting, up from the 16K used for WSJ alone. The setup follows [37], which this paper does not re-describe.

citedFrom.refText: Vinyals, Kaiser, Koo, Petrov, Sutskever & Hinton. Grammar as a foreign language. 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The tree-linearization scheme, the semi-supervised corpora (high-confidence and BerkeleyParser, ~17M sentences), and the RNN seq2seq baselines the Transformer is compared against are all defined in [37].

concepts.name: Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (RNNG)
concepts.summary: A parsing model that builds trees with explicit tree-structured operations; the one prior model the Transformer does not beat on parsing.
concepts.explanation:
RNNG is a model designed specifically for parsing, not a general sequence model pointed at the task. It generates a sentence and its tree jointly, through a sequence of tree-building actions, so the tree structure is baked into the architecture rather than left for the model to imitate in a flat token stream.

It appears in this paper in one role only: the strongest baseline. Among previously reported parsing results, RNNG's is the single one the Transformer's numbers do not exceed.

citedFrom.refText: Dyer, Kuncoro, Ballesteros & Smith. Recurrent neural network grammars. NAACL 2016.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Only needed as the identity of the one baseline that remains ahead; its mechanism is not used by this paper.

concepts.name: BerkeleyParser
concepts.summary: A classical (non-neural) grammar-based parser used as a baseline; the Transformer beats it even with only 40K WSJ training sentences.
concepts.explanation:
The BerkeleyParser is a pre-neural statistical parser. It works by taking a probabilistic grammar and learning refinements of its symbols, rather than by learning continuous representations of words and phrases.

Its role in this paper is as a benchmark for the small-data claim. RNN sequence-to-sequence parsers had been tried in that same setting and had failed to beat it when trained only on the 40K-sentence WSJ set. The Transformer, trained in that same regime, outperforms it.

The name does double duty here. It also labels one of the machine-parsed corpora used in the semi-supervised setting, where the parser supplies automatically produced training trees rather than serving as the thing to beat.

citedFrom.refText: Petrov, Barrett, Thibaux & Klein. Learning accurate, compact, and interpretable tree annotation. ACL 2006.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Only needed as baseline identity; its internals are not used by this paper.
